## Why small interfaces win

The best library I have ever used exposed four functions. The worst exposed four hundred, and its documentation was a tour of every decision its authors had refused to make. An API is a promise about what a caller needs to understand, and a short promise is easier to keep.

This is not an argument for minimalism as taste. It is an argument about cost. Every public function in a library is something that cannot be renamed without breaking someone, cannot be removed without a deprecation cycle, and must be documented, tested, and explained to a new engineer during onboarding. The Unix designers understood this in 1973 when they made a file a stream of bytes and nothing more.

When I review a design, I ask the author to list the things a user must learn before the library is useful. If the list runs past a page, the interface is not finished.

labels.notes: Clean technical essay. "its documentation" and "its authors" are correct possessives.
